Unfortunately, there aren't easy answers to these questions.

> 1. There are potentially 8 QTLS, with a lot of possible interactions from scantwo. I used fitqtl and makeqtl, with the formula of Q1+Q2+...+Q8+Q1:Q2+..+Q7:Q8, I got only one QTL (Q3) have P value<0.05 from both Chi and F test, and 4 more QTL or interactions with P<0.05 only from Chi test. So I am assuming only Q3 is real, right? But by looking at the addint as you suggested. I got two QTL interactions including three QTLs (one was Q3) with one at 0.001 and another at 0.05 Significant (from both Chi and F test). So, What indeed are the QTLs when combining all these tests?

I wouldn't pay too much attention to the p-values that fitqtl gives, as they don't account for the search across the genome.

You could start with the large model and then drop terms, one at a time, until what you're left with seems to have good support. This is the approach used by stepwiseqtl(): use forward selection to a large model followed by backward elimination, and then pick the model that optimizes a penalized LOD score. See Manichaikul et al (2009), http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19104078

> 2. I am not sure if I should only consider first order and pairwise interactions or should add three way or higher terms. When I add Q1*Q2*...Q8, the computer crashed. So  I read the rqtl book, on page 263 it seemed like if there were higher level interactions (for example three way interactions, all three QTL involved into the reaction should also be significant at both first order and pairwise levels. So if I set the formula at Q1*Q2*Q3, if the three-way interaction is true, all QTLs and their interactions should all be Significant at least at the 0.05 level for both Chi and F test, right? Otherwise, it is not a real three-way interaction?

R/qtl currently only deals with pairwise interactions; fitqtl will refuse to consider higher-order interactions.

> 3. I got confused because every time I set different formula (formula1: Q2+Q2+Q3...+Q8+Q1:Q2+...+Q7:Q8, formula 2: Q3+all possible QTL interactions suggested from scantwo, formula 3: all QTLs including qtl interactions from the same chromosomes, which makes a total qtl of 13), I got different results (by only looking at the Chi test and F test). I just don't know where I should start from the scantwo results, is there a general guideline?
> Should I start from the first order, or first order plus pairwise? or else?

I'd start with the main QTL plus a selection of potentially interesting pairwise interactions.

karl

messages.body_plain:
stepwiseqtl can't perform an exhaustive search; if it visited the two QTL with one interaction model, and if the penalized LOD score (with the indicated penalties) was larger than the null, than it would be the selected result. But if it didn't visit that model, then it won't be able to select it.

But with the penalties indicated (2.59, 10.46, 17.81) and the results you showed in a previous email (for the two locus model with QTL on chr 3 and 6), the preferred model would be the single-locus one, with a QTL on chr 3. The LOD score for the second locus with interaction is <<  main + interaction penalty.

karl

messages.subject: How to save imputed genotypes from sim.geno?
messages.subject_clean: How to save imputed genotypes from sim.geno?
messages.body_plain:
I got the following question and I thought others might be interested.

> I have a question about sim.geno in R/QTL. Is there a way to save the imputations of missing genotypes into a cross file along with the observed marker data?
>
> I want to be able to use both the observed marker data plus the imputed genotypes to calculate relative risks of disease from having certain genotypes (or lacking protective alleles) at our QTL. In order to do this, I need to count the three genotypes for both the disease and normal groups.  I tried every thing I could think of to get the data out of those cross$geno lists but was unsuccessful. Hopefully, you will be able to point me in the right direction.

If you want to just save the data for later use within R, you can use save():

  save(mycross, file="mycross.RData")

Later, you'll load it with load("mycross.RData").  Also look at saveRDS() and readRDS().

If you want to pull out the imputations for other uses, see pull.draws().

karl

messages.subject: Re: mqmpermutation takes too long
messages.subject_clean: mqmpermutation takes too long
messages.body_plain:
Dear Gill,

The time and memory requirement for mqmaugment is depending on the amount of missing genotype data in your cross, and also how the data is missing (random versus selective genotyping)
The augmentation does add a power to detect QTLs, but can easily be swapped by a call to the R/qtl function fill.geno

About permutation: this should take a linear amount of time compared to the MQMscan, e.g. if the mqmscan takes 2 hours, 1000 permutations will take ~ 2000 hours.

There isn't really anthing that can be done about that (well one can use less permutations, but the thresholds will be a little bit more variable between runs). The main thing you could try to do to speed up both the initial QTL scan and the permutation is to use less markers as cofactors during the analysis, since the backward elimination step (normally) takes the most time.

Hope this helps,
Danny Arends

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] MQM & Selective Genotyping
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] MQM & Selective Genotyping
messages.body_plain:
With selectively genotyped data (where you genotype just the top and bottom portion of individuals, by phenotype), one can just study the genotyped individuals, but this leads to severe bias in the estimated QTL effects.

Ideally, one considers all individuals (including those phenotyped but not genotyped), but this requires a method that can take proper account of the missing genotypes. For example, Haley-Knott regression (method="hk") performs very poorly in this case. And with the imputation method (method="imp"), one would need to do quite a lot of imputations.

The MQM method has a different kind of trouble with selective genotyping. Its approach to handle missing genotypes is to "augment" the individuals with multiple copies of them, considering all possible values for the unobserved genotypes. In the analysis, these multiple copies are weighted by their probabilities. But with selective genotyping, there are too far many copies that need to be considered in the augmentation.

So selective genotyping is fine in general, but one needs to be careful about the particular method used in trying to account for the missing genotypes.

karl

messages.subject: Detection of QTL in "Connected populations" using R/qtl
messages.subject_clean: Detection of QTL in "Connected populations" using R/qtl
messages.body_plain:
Can R/qtl be used to conduct a QTL analysis (interval mapping) for a set of F2 populations that were created by using a single (hub) female parent that was mated to several (different) male parents?

I have a several sets of these (essentially half-sib-related F2 populations (i.e., Hub Parent A to Parents 1,2,3,4,5,6;  Hub Parent B to Parents 7,8,9,10; and so on, that have been phenotyped and partly genotyped.

The reason I ask this question is that half-sib population sets (like the ones I describe above) are not uncommon in crop plant species and are often the first step populations created for a hub parent in which a breeder is interested to transferring promising traits in the non-hub parent to the hub parent (because that parent is quite valuable in its own right, and the breeder just wants to tinker with improving the Hub parent to make it more valuable.

The use of “connected” populations was described in this publication several years ago:

Blanc et al. 2006. Connected populations for detecting quantitative trait loci and testing for epistasis: an application in maize. TAG 113:206-224.

I was hoping that some simple-to-use software would be developed by now to preform what the above authors describe in their M&M section.  I am absolutely pathetic when it comes to programming code to do this.

So, if this kind of “connected population” QTL detection can be done using R/qtl (as it currently exists) or with some added R-script that would get there, that would be great!

Jim

messages.subject: How does rqtl behave when the allele distribution at one locus is widely different from the expected one?
messages.subject_clean: How does rqtl behave when the allele distribution at one locus is widely different from the expected one?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am analysing an intercross of mice characterized by different susceptibility to induced lung tumorigenesis depending on the genotype at a single major locus. In detail, mice that are "aa" at this locus generally don't develop lung tumors after treatment with a chemical mutagen, while "AA" and "Aa" mice develop from 3-4 to 30 lung tumors per individual.

In this intercross, we are carrying out an eQTL study in lung tumor tissue to find out if the expression levels of specific genes are under quantitative control of the tumor-susceptibility locus. However, since "aa" mice develop lung tumors only in rare cases, we only characterized 8 "aa" lung tumor tissue samples versus around 60 "AA" (each from a different mouse) and 60 "Aa". This means that - only at this locus - our population does not respect the expected genotype frequency.

My question is: Rqtl finds many more statistically significant eQTLs (around 800 target genes) at this locus than for any other locus in the genome (the median of targets per locus is around 5-10). While this can have a biological meaning (the different tumor susceptibility of our cross is mediated by this locus and we are examining gene expression in tumor tissue), I have some doubts that rqtl is somehow getting "confused" by the wrong genotype distribution. Indeed, when I examine the expression levels of the target genes of this locus, I often observe that there is no difference at all between the distribution of the expression levels in AA and Aa mice, while aa mice have only slightly different expression levels, with a very wide distribution (probably due to the very small number of sampled individuals). For instance, in the attached example, rqtl finds a QTL with LOD 9 at this locus (significance threshold with 10,000 perms = 4.5), but I think that the variation of the expression levels is questionable.

Does anyone have any idea on this?

Thank you very much!

Chiara
